title: What If You Could Breathe Liquid? Mice Already Did

scenes.text: What if you could breathe liquid? Mice already have, and it almost worked.
In the 1960s, scientists showed that mice and rats could survive submerged in a fluid called perfluorocarbon.
It holds far more oxygen than water, and rats stayed under for up to 20 hours.
But there's a catch. Liquid is thick, and clearing carbon dioxide takes about 5 liters of fluid a minute at rest.
That climbs to about 10 liters a minute when you move, more than human lungs can pump.
So no one is diving in it yet. But doctors have used it to partly fill the lungs of very sick premature babies.

description:
What if you could breathe liquid?
Mice and rats survived in an oxygen-rich fluid called perfluorocarbon, but human lungs can't move enough of it to clear carbon dioxide.
What should we run through next?
